stem: A Multinational Corporation (MNC) is a company that:
options: Operates only in its home country
Owns or controls production in more than one nation
solution: A Multinational Corporation (MNC) is a company that owns or controls production in more than one nation; MNCs set up offices and factories for production in regions where they can get cheap labour and other resources.

stem: MNCs set up production units (offices and factories) in regions where they can get:
options: Cheap labour and other resources, so that the cost of production is low and the MNCs can earn greater profits
solution: MNCs set up offices and factories for production in regions where they can get cheap labour and other resources; this is done so that the cost of production is low and the MNCs can earn greater profits.

stem: The money that is spent to buy assets such as land, building, machines and other equipment is called:
solution: The money that is spent to buy assets such as land, building, machines and other equipment is called investment.

stem: Investment made by MNCs is called:
solution: Investment made by MNCs is called foreign investment; any investment is made with the hope that these assets will earn profits.

stem: The most common route for MNC investments is to buy up local companies and then to expand production. MNCs with huge wealth can do this quite easily. An example given in the chapter is Cargill Foods, a very large American MNC, which has bought over which Indian company?
solution: MNCs set up production jointly with some of the local companies; sometimes MNCs buy up local companies and then expand production. With huge wealth, this is easy — for example, Cargill Foods, a very large American MNC, has bought over Parakh Foods, an Indian company. Cargill is now the largest producer of edible oil in India.

stem: Besides buying up companies, MNCs also place orders for production with small producers. Garments, footwear and sports items are examples of industries where production is carried out by a large number of small producers around the world. In this arrangement, the products are supplied to the MNCs, which then:
options: Sell these under their own brand names to the customers
solution: Garments, footwear, sports items are examples of industries where production is carried out by a large number of small producers around the world; the products are supplied to the MNCs, which then sell these under their own brand names to the customers. MNCs have tremendous power to determine price, quality, delivery, and labour conditions for these distant producers.

stem: The process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries is called:
solution: Globalisation is the process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries. MNCs are playing a major role in the globalisation process; more and more goods and services, investments and technology are moving between countries.

stem: MNCs are playing a major role in the globalisation process. What is being connected/spread across countries through them?
options: Goods and services, investments and technology between countries
solution: More and more goods and services, investments and technology are moving between countries; MNCs are a major force connecting countries, or connecting distant regions, in the process of globalisation.

stem: Most regions of the world are being connected. Foreign trade is the main channel connecting different countries. Foreign trade provides an opportunity for producers to:
options: Reach beyond the domestic markets, i.e., markets of their own countries
solution: Foreign trade creates an opportunity for the producers to reach beyond the domestic markets, i.e., markets of their own countries; producers can sell their produce not only in markets located within the country but can also compete in markets located in other countries.

stem: Foreign trade results in connecting the markets or integration of markets in different countries. What is one effect on buyers?
options: Buyers have a choice of goods beyond what is produced domestically; the choice of goods in the markets rises
solution: For buyers, imports of goods produced in another country is one way of expanding the choice of goods beyond what is domestically produced. With the opening of trade, goods travel from one market to another; producers in two countries closely compete against each other even though they are separated by thousands of miles.

stem: Foreign trade thus results in connecting the markets or integration of markets in different countries. What tends to happen to prices of similar goods in the two countries?
options: They tend to become equal (price of similar goods in the two markets tends to become equal)
solution: Foreign trade results in connecting the markets or integration of markets in different countries; the price of similar goods in the two markets tends to become equal, and producers in the two countries closely compete against each other.

stem: Several factors have enabled globalisation. The most important among these has been:
options: Rapid improvement in technology, especially in transportation and information and communication technology
solution: Several factors have enabled globalisation; rapid improvement in technology has been one major factor that has stimulated the globalisation process — particularly improvement in transportation technology, which has made much faster delivery of goods across long distances possible at lower costs.

stem: In recent times, technology in the areas of telecommunications, computers and the Internet has been changing rapidly. Telecommunication facilities (telegraph, telephone including mobile phones, fax) are used to:
options: Contact one another around the world, to access information instantly, and to communicate from remote areas
solution: Telecommunication facilities are used to contact one another around the world, to access information instantly, and to communicate from remote areas. This has been facilitated by satellite communication devices.

stem: Computers have now entered almost every field of activity. As you might be aware of the extensive use of the internet, this allows us to:
options: Obtain and share information on almost anything we want to know, and to communicate through email, voice-mail, etc., across the world at negligible costs
solution: The Internet allows us to obtain and share information on almost anything we want to know; it also enables us to communicate through email, voice-mail, etc., across the world at negligible costs. Amazing! A News magazine published for London readers can be designed and printed in Delhi, and airlifted to London.

stem: Information and communication technology (IT) has played a major role in spreading out production of services across countries. Which services can now be done through IT and shifted to distant countries?
options: Data entry, accounting, administrative tasks, engineering, and even 'call centre' services
solution: IT has played a major role in spreading out production of services across countries; a company's administrative and even engineering jobs can now be done cheaply in countries like India and be exported back. Similarly, data entry, accounting, and 'call centre' services can be located far from the country where the goods and services are sold.

stem: Before globalisation, the Indian government had put barriers to foreign trade and foreign investment. This was considered necessary at that time to:
options: Protect the producers within the country from foreign competition, especially because industries were just coming up in the 1950s and 1960s
solution: The Indian government had put barriers to foreign trade and foreign investment; this was considered necessary to protect the producers within the country from foreign competition. Industries were just coming up in the 1950s and 1960s, and competition from imports at that stage would not have allowed these industries to come up.

stem: A tax on imports is an example of a trade barrier. It is called a trade barrier because:
options: Some restriction has been set up (a 'barrier') on the free movement of goods across countries; governments can use it to increase or decrease foreign trade and to decide what kinds of goods should come in
solution: Tax on imports is an example of a trade barrier; it is called a barrier because some restriction has been set up. Governments can use trade barriers to increase or decrease (regulate) foreign trade and to decide what kinds of goods and how much of each should come into the country.

stem: The Indian government allowed only essential items such as machinery, fertilisers, petroleum etc. to be imported. Around 1991, some far-reaching changes in policy were made. India decided that the time had come for Indian producers to:
options: Compete with producers around the globe; competition would improve the performance of producers within the country
solution: Starting around 1991, India decided that the time had come for Indian producers to compete with producers around the globe; it was felt that competition would improve the performance of producers within the country since they would have to improve their quality.

stem: Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government is what is known as:
solution: Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government is what is known as liberalisation. With liberalisation of trade, businesses are allowed to make decisions freely about what they wish to import or export.

stem: With liberalisation of trade, businesses are allowed to make decisions freely about what they wish to import or export. The government imposes:
options: Much less restrictions than before, and is therefore said to be more liberal
solution: With liberalisation, the government imposes much less restrictions than before and is therefore said to be more liberal. Businesses can decide freely what to import or export; earlier the government had permitted imports of only certain goods.

stem: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) is an organisation whose aim is to:
options: Liberalise international trade — it establishes rules regarding international trade and sees that these rules are obeyed
solution: The WTO is one such organisation whose aim is to liberalise international trade. Started at the initiative of the developed countries, the WTO establishes rules regarding international trade, and sees that these rules are obeyed. About 164 countries of the world are currently members of the WTO.

stem: Though the WTO is supposed to allow free trade for all, in practice it is seen that:
options: The developed countries have unfairly retained trade barriers (e.g., on agriculture), while the WTO rules have forced developing countries to remove theirs
solution: Though WTO is supposed to allow free trade for all, in practice, it is seen that the developed countries have unfairly retained trade barriers. On the other hand, WTO rules have forced the developing countries to remove trade barriers. An example is the current debate on trade in agricultural products.

stem: Globalisation and greater competition among producers has been advantageous to consumers, particularly the well-off sections in the urban areas. There is greater choice before these consumers who now enjoy:
options: Improved quality and lower prices for several products, and enjoy much higher standards of living
solution: For consumers, particularly the well-off sections in the urban areas, there is a greater choice; they now enjoy improved quality and lower prices for several products. As a result, these people today enjoy much higher standards of living than was possible earlier.

stem: MNCs have increased their investments in India over the past 20 years, which means investing in India has been:
options: Profitable/beneficial for them, and MNCs have been interested in industries such as cell phones, automobiles, electronics, soft drinks, fast food, or services such as banking
solution: MNCs have increased their investments in India over the past 20 years, which means investing in India has been beneficial for them. MNCs have been interested in industries such as cell phones, automobiles, electronics, soft drinks, fast food or services such as banking in urban areas; these products have a large number of well-off buyers.

stem: New jobs have been created for people with the coming of MNCs, particularly in the services sector such as IT. Some large Indian companies have also benefited from globalisation and have become:
options: Multinationals themselves — e.g., Tata Motors, Infosys, Ranbaxy, Asian Paints
solution: Globalisation has also created new opportunities for companies providing services, particularly those involving IT. Several of the top Indian companies have been able to benefit from the increased competition; they have invested in newer technology and production methods and raised their production standards. Some have gained from successful collaborations with foreign companies, and several Indian companies have emerged as multinationals themselves — e.g., Tata Motors, Infosys, Ranbaxy, Asian Paints, Sundram Fasteners.

stem: Globalisation has enabled some large Indian companies to emerge as multinationals. It has also created new opportunities for companies providing services, particularly those involving:
solution: Globalisation has created new opportunities for companies providing services, particularly those involving IT. The Indian company producing a magazine for the London-based company and call centres are some examples. Besides, a host of services such as data entry, accounting, administrative tasks, engineering are now being done cheaply in countries such as India and exported to developed countries.

stem: Globalisation has not been beneficial for all. The impact of globalisation has NOT been uniform. Which group has NOT gained much from globalisation?
options: Small producers and workers, especially those who have faced tough competition from imports or unstable, low-paid employment
solution: Globalisation has not been beneficial for all; the impact of globalisation has not been uniform. While consumers and producers with skill, education and wealth have benefited, small producers (e.g., batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy products, and vegetable oil) have been hurt by competition, and many faced ruin and job losses.

stem: Several of the Indian small industries have been hit hard by competition. Rising competition means most employers these days prefer to employ workers 'flexibly'. This means:
options: Workers' jobs are no longer secure — workers are employed only when needed, and denied fair wages and benefits
solution: To compete, most employers these days prefer to employ workers 'flexibly'; this means that workers' jobs are no longer secure. Workers are employed flexibly and denied their fair share of benefits brought about by globalisation.

stem: In order to compete in the market, employers cut labour costs. Workers in the unorganised sector are the worst hit. For example, in the garment export industry, workers are:
options: Given permanent jobs with high pay
Employed on a temporary basis, made to work long hours, and paid low wages
solution: The flexibility in labour laws means workers are hired for short periods, made to work long hours, and paid low wages. For example, in the ready-made garments industry, employers hire workers only when there are orders and remove them when work is over, without job security or benefits — the workers bear the burden of competition.

stem: The demand for a 'fair globalisation' is that its benefits should be:
options: Shared better and made more fair by creating opportunities for all, and ensuring that the benefits are shared better
solution: The pressure of competition has substantially changed the lives of workers; fair globalisation would create opportunities for all, and also ensure that the benefits of globalisation are shared better. Globalisation must be made more 'fair' so that its benefits reach everyone.

stem: The government can play a major role in making globalisation fair. Which of the following is a step the government can take?
options: Ensuring that labour laws are properly implemented and the workers get their rights
solution: The government can play a major role in making globalisation fair. Its policies must protect the interests, not only of the rich and powerful, but of all the people in the country. The government can ensure that labour laws are properly implemented and that workers get their rights.

stem: To make globalisation fair, besides implementing labour laws, the government can also:
options: Support small producers to improve their performance till the time they become strong enough to compete, and use trade and investment barriers if necessary
solution: The government can support small producers to improve their performance till the time they become strong enough to compete. If necessary, the government can use trade and investment barriers. It can negotiate at the WTO for 'fairer rules', and can also align with other developing countries with similar interests to fight against the domination of developed countries in the WTO.

stem: The government can negotiate at the WTO for 'fairer rules'. It can also align with other developing countries with similar interests to:
options: Fight against the domination of developed countries in the WTO
solution: The government can negotiate at the WTO for 'fairer rules'; it can also align with other developing countries with similar interests to fight against the domination of developed countries in the WTO. This is one way the interests of workers and small producers can be protected in a globalised world.

stem: Fair globalisation implies which of the following about the sharing of benefits?
options: Only MNCs and rich should benefit
The benefits of globalisation should be shared by all sections of society, including workers and small producers, not just the well-off
Benefits should go to foreign countries
solution: Fair globalisation would create opportunities for all, and also ensure that the benefits of globalisation are shared better — reaching workers, small producers and the poor, not just the well-off consumers, large companies and MNCs.

stem: Which of the following is the correct sequence in which an MNC decides where to set up production?
options: Regions/countries which are close to the markets, where there is cheap labour and other resources, and where government policies are favourable
solution: MNCs set up production where it is close to the markets; where there is skilled and unskilled labour available at low costs; and where the availability of other factors of production is assured. They also look for government policies that protect their interests. Cost of production is the key consideration.

stem: MNCs set up production jointly with local companies. The benefit to the local company of such joint production is:
options: MNCs can provide money for additional investments, and bring with them the latest technology for production
solution: The benefit to the local company of joint production is two-fold: first, MNCs can provide money for additional investments, like buying new machines for faster production; second, MNCs might bring with them the latest technology for production.

stem: Foreign investment by MNCs and the spread of their production and interlinking of production across countries have been an important feature of the current phase of globalisation. This has been made possible by:
options: Liberalisation of foreign trade and foreign investment policies, and improvements in transport and communication technology
solution: Foreign investment by MNCs and the interlinking of production across countries has been made possible by the liberalisation of foreign trade and foreign investment policies in many countries, along with rapid improvements in transportation and communication (IT) technology, which reduced the cost and increased the speed of moving goods, services, and information.

stem: The chapter explains that globalisation has interlinked production across countries. A finished product like a car may have parts made in many countries. This shows that production is:
options: Increasingly organised in complex ways spread across the countries, with MNCs controlling production across nations
solution: Production across countries is increasingly interlinked; a large MNC may be spread across many countries, with different processes and parts of production organised in different locations to take advantage of low costs. MNCs control production spread across nations, a defining feature of modern globalisation.

stem: Which of the following would be an example of a trade barrier being reduced through liberalisation?
options: Increasing the tax on imported goods
Reducing or removing the tax on imports so that more foreign goods can come in
solution: Liberalisation involves reducing or removing trade barriers such as taxes on imports; when the import tax is reduced or removed, more foreign goods can come into the country and businesses are free to decide what to import or export.

stem: The rapid movement of goods across large distances at low cost has been made possible mainly by improvements in:
options: Transportation technology, including containers and faster ships and aircraft
solution: The rapid movement of goods across large distances has been made possible by improvements in transportation technology — the development of containers for transport, and faster and cheaper ships and aircraft — which has enabled much faster delivery of goods across long distances at lower costs.

stem: Consumers in India today have a wider choice of goods and better quality partly because of:
options: The entry of foreign companies and imported goods due to globalisation and liberalisation
solution: Because of globalisation and liberalisation, foreign companies have entered India and imported goods are available; this greater competition has given consumers, particularly well-off urban consumers, a wider choice of goods and services, often at better quality and lower prices.

stem: Which of the following statements about the impact of globalisation on workers is correct?
options: Workers, particularly in the unorganised sector, have often faced job insecurity and low wages due to flexible employment, even as some skilled workers gained
Globalisation has no effect on workers
solution: The impact of globalisation on workers has been uneven; while some skilled and educated workers gained new opportunities (especially in IT), a large number of workers, particularly in the unorganised sector, faced job insecurity, flexible employment, long hours, and low wages, as employers cut labour costs to compete.

stem: The main reason MNCs are able to control production even by small producers in distant countries (like garments) is that:
options: MNCs are the largest buyers, and by placing large orders they can determine the price, quality, delivery and labour conditions for these producers
Small producers have no choice legally
solution: Large MNCs in developed countries place orders for production with small producers; the garments, footwear and sports items are made by small producers who then supply to MNCs. Since the MNCs are the largest buyers, they have tremendous power to determine the price, quality, delivery, and labour conditions for these distant producers.

stem: The overall conclusion about globalisation the chapter reaches is that:
options: It has benefited some (well-off consumers, skilled workers, large companies) but not others (small producers and workers), and must be made 'fairer' so that its benefits are shared by all
solution: The chapter concludes that globalisation has led to greater integration of economies and has benefited well-off consumers, skilled and educated workers, MNCs, and some large Indian companies. However, its benefits have not been uniform — small producers and many workers have not gained much. Hence there is a need for 'fair globalisation', where the government ensures benefits are shared by all.

stem: The number of member countries in the WTO (World Trade Organisation) is approximately:
solution: About 164 countries of the world are currently members of the WTO; it was started at the initiative of the developed countries and aims to liberalise international trade by establishing rules and seeing that they are obeyed.

stem: Which of the following pairs of policy terms is correctly explained?
options: Liberalisation — removing government restrictions/barriers on trade and investment; Globalisation — integration between countries
Trade barrier — free movement of goods
solution: Liberalisation means removing barriers or restrictions set by the government (on trade and investment), making the government more 'liberal'. Globalisation is the process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries. Liberalisation of trade and investment policies has helped the globalisation process.

stem: A key reason India removed many trade barriers around 1991 was the belief that:
options: Competition would improve the performance of producers within the country by forcing them to improve quality
Indian producers did not need to improve
solution: Around 1991, India decided that the time had come for Indian producers to compete with producers around the globe; it was felt that competition would improve the performance of producers within the country, since they would be forced to improve their quality and efficiency to survive.

stem: The role of foreign investment and MNCs in creating jobs in India is best described as:
options: Creating new jobs, especially in urban areas and the services/IT sector, though not benefiting all sections equally
solution: MNCs and foreign investment have created new jobs in India, particularly in urban areas and in the services sector such as IT; however, the benefits have not been uniform, as small producers and many workers in the unorganised sector have not gained equally and some have lost their livelihoods.

stem: The most important role the government should play in a globalised economy, according to the chapter, is to ensure that its policies protect:
options: The interests not only of the rich and powerful, but of all the people in the country
solution: The government can play a major role in making globalisation fair; its policies must protect the interests, not only of the rich and powerful, but of all the people in the country — including workers and small producers — so that the benefits of globalisation reach everyone.

stem: The money spent to buy assets such as land, buildings, machines and other equipment is called:
solution: The money that is spent to buy assets such as land, building, machines and other equipment is called investment.

stem: Investment made by MNCs in another country is called:
solution: Investment made by multinational corporations (MNCs) is called foreign investment; MNCs invest to set up or buy production units in other countries.

stem: The main channel connecting countries through globalisation, in which markets in different countries become integrated, is:
solution: Foreign trade is the main channel connecting countries; it creates an opportunity for producers to reach beyond domestic markets, and integrates the markets of different countries.

stem: The single most important factor that has stimulated the globalisation process is:
solution: The rapid improvement in technology has been one of the major factors stimulating the globalisation process, especially in transportation, telecommunications and information technology.

stem: The technology in telecommunications, computers and the internet, which has enabled globalisation, is together called:
solution: Information and communication technology (IT) — telecommunications, computers and the internet — has played a major role in spreading production of services across countries and connecting markets.

stem: A tax imposed by a government on imports is an example of a trade barrier called:
solution: A tax on imports is an example of a trade barrier; such a tax is called a tariff (or customs duty), used by governments to regulate foreign trade and protect domestic producers.

stem: The removal of barriers or restrictions set by the government on trade is known as:
solution: Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government on foreign trade and investment is known as liberalisation; with liberalisation, businesses are allowed to make their own decisions freely.

stem: The Indian government began removing many barriers to foreign trade and investment around the year:
solution: Around 1991, the Indian government decided to remove many of the barriers to foreign trade and foreign investment, believing that Indian producers were ready to compete with producers around the globe.

stem: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) is an international organisation whose main aim is to:
options: Liberalise international trade and lay down rules for it
solution: The WTO is an organisation whose aim is to liberalise international trade; it establishes rules regarding international trade and sees that these rules are obeyed by member nations.

stem: Though the WTO is meant to allow free trade for all, in practice its rules have often:
options: Been unfair to developing countries, while developed countries kept some protections
solution: Though the WTO is supposed to allow free trade, in practice developed countries have unfairly retained trade barriers (like subsidies to farmers), while pressuring developing countries to remove theirs.

stem: When a developed country continues to give large subsidies to its farmers while asking developing countries to remove trade barriers, it shows that:
options: WTO rules have sometimes been unfair to developing countries
solution: Developed countries have unfairly retained large agricultural subsidies and used their power in the WTO to their advantage, showing that the practice of 'free and fair trade' has often disadvantaged developing countries.

stem: Globalisation and greater competition have generally benefited:
options: Consumers, especially the well-off, with more choice and better quality at lower prices
solution: Globalisation and greater competition among producers have been advantageous to consumers, particularly the well-off sections in urban areas, who now enjoy greater choice, improved quality and lower prices.

stem: New jobs created by MNCs coming to India are especially found in sectors such as:
solution: The coming of MNCs and globalisation has created new jobs, particularly in information technology, and services such as call centres, benefiting people with the required skills.

stem: Globalisation has also enabled some large Indian companies to emerge as:
solution: Globalisation has enabled some large Indian companies (like Tata Motors, Infosys, and Ranbaxy) to emerge as multinationals themselves, spreading their operations across many countries.

stem: Assertion (A): Small producers and workers have often been hurt by globalisation. Reason (R): They face stiff competition from cheaper imports and MNC products, and employers cut labour costs.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Many small Indian industries (batteries, plastics, tyres, dairy, edible oil) have been hit by competition, and to compete, employers cut labour costs by hiring workers 'flexibly' — R explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): The Indian government liberalised trade around 1991. Reason (R): It believed Indian producers were ready to compete with producers around the world.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: India removed many trade barriers around 1991 because it believed that competition would improve the quality and performance of Indian producers, who were now ready to compete globally — R explains A.

stem: To compete in the global market, employers often cut labour costs by:
options: Employing workers 'flexibly' for short periods with low wages and no security
solution: To reduce costs and stay competitive, employers increasingly employ workers 'flexibly' — for short periods, when there is intense pressure of work — with low wages, long hours and no job security, hurting workers.

stem: To make globalisation fair, the government can:
options: Ensure labour laws are implemented and support small producers
solution: The government can make globalisation fair by ensuring that labour laws are properly implemented and workers get their rights, and by supporting small producers to improve their performance until they become strong enough to compete.

stem: To make globalisation fairer at the international level, the government can:
options: Negotiate at the WTO for fairer rules and align with other developing countries
solution: The government can negotiate at the WTO for 'fairer rules' and can also align with other developing countries with similar interests to fight against the domination of developed countries in the WTO.

stem: The most common route for MNCs to spread their production is to:
options: Buy up local companies and then expand production
Only build entirely new factories alone
solution: One of the most common routes for MNC investments is to buy up local companies and then expand production; MNCs with abundant wealth can easily do so.

stem: Besides buying up companies, MNCs also control production by:
options: Placing orders with small producers who supply goods to them
solution: MNCs place orders for production with small producers — for garments, footwear, sports items, etc. The products are supplied to the MNCs, which sell these under their own brand names, controlling the production process.

stem: Match the term with its meaning: (i) Liberalisation (ii) Tariff (iii) Foreign investment — (a) tax on imports (b) removal of trade barriers (c) money invested by MNCs abroad:
solution: Liberalisation is the removal of trade barriers, a tariff is a tax on imports, and foreign investment is money invested by MNCs in another country.

stem: MNCs choose to set up production units in a region considering factors such as:
options: Cheap labour, proximity to markets, and availability of skilled workers and infrastructure
solution: MNCs set up production where it is close to markets, where there is cheap and skilled labour, and where other factors of production and government policies (favourable) are available, to keep costs low and profits high.

stem: When an MNC sets up production jointly with a local company, the local company benefits from:
options: Additional investment and the latest technology for production
solution: When MNCs set up production jointly with local companies, the local company benefits in two ways: MNCs provide money for additional investment, and they bring with them the latest technology for production.

stem: The integration of production and markets across countries is the central feature of:
solution: Globalisation is the process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries; MNCs are playing a major role by integrating production and connecting markets across the world.

stem: The rapid movement of goods across large distances at low cost has been made possible chiefly by improvements in:
options: Transportation technology (containers, faster ships and aircraft)
solution: Developments in transportation technology, such as containers and faster and cheaper shipping and air transport, have made the movement of goods across long distances much quicker and cheaper.

stem: Before liberalisation, the Indian government allowed the import of only:
options: Essential items like machinery, fertilisers and petroleum
solution: Before liberalisation, the government allowed imports of only essential items such as machinery, fertilisers and petroleum, and placed barriers on the import of most consumer goods to protect domestic producers.

stem: Consumers in India today enjoy the benefits of globalisation in the form of:
options: A wider choice of goods with better quality and often lower prices
solution: For consumers, especially the rich in urban areas, globalisation has brought a wider variety of goods (like cars, electronics, food) with improved quality and often lower prices, along with higher standards of living.

stem: The main reason MNCs are able to control production even by small distant producers is that:
options: They are large and powerful buyers who dictate price, quality and delivery conditions
solution: MNCs, being large and powerful, place bulk orders and control the terms of production — the price, quality, delivery and labour conditions — so small producers who depend on these orders must comply.

stem: The distinction between foreign trade and foreign investment is that foreign trade involves the movement of goods and services, while foreign investment involves:
options: The buying of assets (like factories) in another country
solution: Foreign trade involves the exchange of goods and services between countries, whereas foreign investment involves the purchase of assets such as land, buildings and machines in a foreign country by MNCs.

stem: Which of the following best states the overall conclusion of the chapter about globalisation?
options: Globalisation has benefited many but not all; it should be made fairer
solution: The chapter concludes that globalisation has benefited well-off consumers and skilled, educated producers, but has hurt many small producers and workers; hence there is a need to make globalisation 'fair' so that its benefits are shared more equitably.

stem: Small industries in India, such as those making batteries, plastics and toys, have been hit hard by globalisation because they:
options: Could not compete with cheaper and better goods from large firms and imports
solution: Several small Indian industries have been unable to compete with the cheaper, better-quality goods produced by MNCs and imports; many have shut down, causing job losses.

stem: Globalisation has interlinked production across countries such that a single product may:
options: Be produced using parts and services from many different countries
Be made entirely in one village
solution: Globalisation has interlinked production across the globe, so that the different stages of producing a single item (such as a car or a phone) may be spread across several countries to minimise costs.

stem: The role of the government in a globalised economy should be to:
options: Ensure that the benefits of globalisation reach all and protect the interests of workers and small producers
solution: The government should play a positive role by making globalisation fair — implementing labour laws, supporting small producers, negotiating fairer trade rules, and ensuring the benefits reach a large section of people.

stem: An example of a trade barrier being removed would be:
options: Reducing or abolishing the tax (tariff) on imported goods
solution: Removing a trade barrier means reducing or abolishing taxes and restrictions on foreign trade, such as lowering the tariff on imported goods so they can enter more freely.

stem: Foreign investment and the spread of MNC production have interlinked the production and markets of different countries, which is the essence of:
solution: The spread of MNC investment and production, along with foreign trade, has interlinked the production processes and markets of different nations — the core of the globalisation process.

stem: Liberalisation of trade means that businesses are allowed to:
options: Freely import and export and make their own decisions
solution: With liberalisation of trade, businesses are allowed to make decisions freely about what they wish to import or export, and the government imposes fewer restrictions than before.

stem: The greater competition brought by globalisation has forced Indian producers to:
options: Improve the quality of their goods to survive
solution: Facing competition from foreign producers, many top Indian companies have benefited by improving the quality and efficiency of their production, investing in new technology and raising standards.

stem: The chapter suggests that the impact of globalisation has NOT been:
solution: The impact of globalisation has not been uniform; it has helped well-off consumers and skilled workers, while creating hardships for many small producers and unorganised workers.

stem: An MNC deciding where to locate production would typically consider countries offering:
options: Cheap labour, resources, markets and favourable government policies
solution: MNCs decide to set up production considering factors like the availability of cheap labour and resources, proximity to markets, and favourable government policies, in order to minimise costs and maximise profits.

stem: Fair globalisation implies that the benefits of globalisation should be:
options: Shared better, giving people better opportunities and protection
solution: Fair globalisation would create opportunities for all, and also ensure that the benefits of globalisation are shared better, with government support and protection for the vulnerable.

stem: The removal of trade barriers by India was intended to allow:
options: Freer flow of foreign goods and investment and more competition
solution: By removing trade barriers, India allowed goods and investment to flow more freely across its borders, increasing competition and integration with the world economy under liberalisation.

stem: The competition among producers due to globalisation benefits consumers by:
options: Lowering prices and improving quality and choice
solution: Greater competition among producers, both local and foreign, benefits consumers who now enjoy a greater choice of goods at lower prices with better quality.

stem: The main role of MNCs in globalisation is that they:
options: Spread their production across countries and connect distant markets
solution: MNCs are central to globalisation because they spread their production across multiple countries and, through foreign trade and investment, connect and integrate markets around the world.

stem: The reason globalisation has been possible in services like customer care is mainly:
options: Information technology allowing services to be delivered across borders
solution: IT has allowed services such as data entry, accounting, and customer-care call centres to be delivered from one country to consumers in another, enabling the globalisation of services.

stem: To protect small producers during globalisation, the government could:
options: Support them with credit, technology and marketing until they can compete
solution: The government can help small producers improve their performance — providing credit, technology and marketing support — until they become strong enough to compete, an important part of fair globalisation.

stem: 'Foreign investment' and 'foreign trade' are distinguished in that foreign trade involves the movement of goods and services between countries, whereas foreign investment involves:
options: MNCs putting money to buy assets such as land, buildings, machines and equipment in another country to set up or control production there
solution: Foreign trade is the buying and selling (import/export) of goods and services across national borders, connecting markets. Foreign investment is the money spent by MNCs to buy assets (land, buildings, machines, equipment) and set up or control production in another country. Both are important channels of globalisation.
